title: Indifference
hookLine: not coldness but freedom: not preferring health to sickness, wealth to poverty, for their own sake

lines: HEALTH OR SICKNESS, RICHES OR POVERTY.
cards: Call someone indifferent today and it's an insult. It means they don't care: the shrug, the blank text back, the person who walks past.

So it's a jolt to find the word in Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises as something to want. In the same paragraph as yesterday's foundation, he says we need to make ourselves indifferent to all created things.

Not wanting health more than sickness, riches more than poverty, honor more than dishonor, a long life more than a short one. Taken one way, that sounds cold, even inhuman. Ignatius means nearly the opposite.

teach.b: None of these things is wanted for its own sake, and Ignatius limits it to what is left to our free choice and not forbidden.
He isn't saying sickness is as good as health, or that nobody should look after a body or pay the rent. He's saying don't let any one of those things own you.
If you need to be healthy, rich and admired no matter what, those needs make your choices for you. You aren't free.
Indifference, for Ignatius, is balance: standing like a scale that hasn't tipped yet, so the only weight that tips it is what God is asking, what serves love.
Then comes the second half of his sentence, which is all desire: we should want and choose only what helps us toward the end we're made for. So indifference isn't wanting nothing.
It's wanting one thing so much that everything else can move.

Paul writes from prison, to the Philippians: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound." Learned, notice. Not born with it.
And a Gospel scene has the same shape: Jesus in the garden the night before he dies. He doesn't pretend he wants the cross. He asks for the cup to pass.

teach.h: NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.
teach.b: And then: "nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." That's not coldness. It's freedom, and a warm kind: a real preference, said out loud, and then held open.

how: In Ignatian spirituality, people making a decision pray first for indifference, the inner freedom to choose whatever best serves God, often with a spiritual director, before weighing the options.

o: inner freedom: no created thing owns your choices
not caring at all what happens to others
accepting whatever comes without any hope

p: a scale that hasn't tipped yet
not as I will, but as thou wilt

s: it means not being owned by any created thing, so you're free to choose love.
the same sentence goes on: want and choose only what helps toward the end we're made for.
in the garden, Jesus says he wants the cross
he asks for the cup to pass, then says not as I will, but as thou wilt.

games.q: you're praying over a decision you care a lot about. what does Ignatius ask first?
o: pretend you don't have a preference.
name your preference, then hold it open so love can tip the scale.
pick the harder option, since it must be holier.
games.why: indifference isn't faking. it's a real preference held loosely, the way Jesus in the garden asks for the cup to pass and then says not as I will.

practice: Choose something you're hoping for right now, a result, a reply, a plan, and let yourself want it honestly; then picture both outcomes and see whether love could still be found in the other one.
If you pray, say the line from the garden, not as I will, but as thou wilt, meaning only as much as you can; if not, let the hope sit beside the other outcome, both in view.

wordCard.voice: Indifference. In Ignatius, not coldness but freedom: wanting nothing created for its own sake, so you're free to choose what serves God and love.

orig.note: Greek: content, having enough within; Paul's word in Philippians 4:11.

carryVoice: Your line: free to choose love. Wanting one thing lets everything else move. Go gently.

sources.ref: Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises §23 (Principle and Foundation)
